sections.body: The box hangs inside the tank on suction cups. A pregnant female sits in the upper chamber. Fry fall through the slotted floor into the lower chamber, where the adult cannot follow. It separates the two at birth without you watching, and because the box shares the tank's water it needs no heater, no extra filter and no second cycle. When the fry are big enough, release them straight into the main tank without any shock.

Do not leave a female in a breeder box for days, since the confinement stresses her and can bring on early or failed births. Move her in only when she is close to dropping, then take her out soon after. Make sure there is some flow through the box, which comes from the tank's own circulation. Place it where the filter outflow gently moves the water but does not blast into it, and drop in a little plant material or a leaf so that fry have cover.

The divided chamber is also a handy isolation box for a fish that needs treating or a torn fin that needs a rest. For fry that are growing out, feed [decapsulated brine shrimp eggs](/product/decapsulated-brine-shrimp-eggs) or finely crushed flake in small amounts, and siphon leftovers so that the box water does not foul.

faqs.q: Which fish is it for?
faqs.a: It suits livebearers such as guppies, mollies and platies, where fry are born live. For egg layers, use it as an isolation or grow-out box.

sections.body: A fixed net is fine until you need the back corner of a deep scape. This one extends on a stainless telescopic handle so you can reach the substrate without putting your arm into the tank, and it collapses to roughly a third of its length for storage. The soft, fine mesh holds shrimp, fry and small fish and will not split a long fin.

Catch fish by herding them into the net with a second tool or a hand, not by chasing. Slow movements and a corner of the tank make it easier. Scoop with a quick, shallow motion and lift the net so that water drains rather than the fish dangling. For shrimp, keep the net in the water as you lift and move the shrimp into a container in the net.

Rinse the net in clean water after use. Do not use soap or detergent, which can harm fish. Keep one net for each tank, or rinse well, so that disease does not move between tanks. If you quarantine fish, use a separate net for the quarantine tank.

faqs.q: Can I use it for shrimplets?
faqs.a: The mesh is fine and soft, which suits shrimp. For very small shrimplets, a scoop with a small container may be gentler.

sections.body: A magnetic cleaner has two halves, one inside the tank and one outside. If they separate mid-clean, a normal inner half sinks into the substrate and drags grit across the glass when you retrieve it. The floating inner half rises instead, so it is easy to catch. That single feature is why these are worth buying.

Most scratched panes come from a grain of sand trapped under the pad, not the pad itself. Keep the cleaner above the substrate line, rinse the pad if it picks up grit, and use the weakest magnet that still moves smoothly. A magnet that is too strong traps debris more tightly against the glass. The pack gives three sizes of grip, so match one to your glass thickness (the pack lists glass up to about 10 mm).

Acrylic scratches much more easily than glass. If you have an acrylic tank, check the cleaner is made for it and test a small patch first. For stubborn spot algae on glass, a scraper blade is more effective than more pressure.

A freshly trimmed stem has no roots, so it has no anchor. Push it into the substrate and it often pops back out within a day or two. These soft strips wrap around the base of a stem bundle and hold it down until roots form. They are the standard fix, and they work on moss and loose trimmings too.

Bundle three to six stems, wrap the strip once or twice around the base and press the ends together. Wrap firmly enough to hold, but not so tight that it crushes the stem, which stops it taking up water. Push the bundle into the substrate until the weight sits on the surface or just under it.

Leave them on until you see white roots, usually after a couple of weeks. Then unwrap and reuse them on the next batch of trimmings. If you leave them on too long, they can restrict a thickening stem. Ten strips is enough to replant a whole tank after a trim.

These submersible LED wands come with a remote and are waterproof for permanent underwater use. They are decorative lighting for display tanks and moody evening scenes, and they can serve as a dim night light for nocturnal species. They are not a plant-growth light, so use them alongside a proper [full-spectrum bar](/product/aurora-48-planted-tank-led) in a planted tank.

Colour lighting on for long hours can feed algae, especially in a tank with spare nutrients. Use them in the evening for an hour or two, or as a dim night mode, and keep your daily plant lighting on a timer. If you keep fish that need real darkness to sleep, turn the wands off at night.

Place the wand behind hardscape or along the back glass so the light glows around objects, rather than shining at the viewer. Hide the cable behind rocks or plants, and route the lead out above the waterline with a drip loop so water cannot run along it to the plug.

faqs.q: Will they grow plants?
faqs.a: No. Colour wands are for effect. Use a full-spectrum light for plants.

faqs.q: Can I leave them on all night?
faqs.a: It is better not to. Most fish and plants benefit from a period of full darkness, and constant light encourages algae.

sections.body: These fast-dissolve tablets are meant for new tanks and for resetting water after a course of medication. The dose is one tablet per 20 litres. Use them as the label says and keep the filter running while they work.

Tablets help with the symptoms, not the cause. Cloudy water usually comes from a bacterial bloom in a new tank, overfeeding, a filter that has been cleaned too hard, or disturbed substrate. Fix the cause by feeding less, rinsing media gently in tank water and giving a new tank time. After medication, a water change and fresh [activated carbon](/product/activated-carbon-filter-bags) are the usual way to clear residue.

Count the litres in your tank after hardscape and substrate, not the label volume. Do not double the dose to clear things faster. Test the water with [test strips](/product/test-strips-8-in-1-100-count) if livestock look stressed, since cloudy water often goes with an ammonia or nitrite spike.

faqs.q: How many tablets for my tank?
faqs.a: One tablet per 20 litres of water, so a 60 litre tank takes three. Count the real water volume.

faqs.q: Do I need to remove the carbon first?
faqs.a: Carbon can remove treatments from the water. If the tablets are meant to stay active, take carbon out while they work, and replace it afterwards.

sections.body: This liquid clarifier is for green or cloudy tanks. It works over 24 to 48 hours with the filter running, and it is safe for plants and shrimp when dosed as directed. Dose by the label, and keep the filter on so that the clumped particles are caught as the water passes through.

White cloud is usually a bacterial bloom in a new tank and clears by itself in a few days. Green water is free-floating algae, usually from too much light or too much nutrient. A clarifier clears either quickly, but if you do not fix the cause the water turns again. Cut the lighting period, reduce feeding, and check your fertiliser dosing in a planted tank.

Clumped particles end up in the filter, so rinse the sponge or replace the [floss pad](/product/aquarium-filter-floss-pad) a day or two after the water clears. If it is a heavily planted tank, a water change after clearing restores any nutrients that were pulled out.

faqs.q: How soon will the water clear?
faqs.a: Typically within 24 to 48 hours with the filter running. A tank with an ongoing cause, such as too much light, may cloud again.

faqs.q: Is it safe for shrimp?
faqs.a: The listing states it is safe for plants and shrimp when dosed as directed. Start with the lower end of the dose in a shrimp tank.

sections.h: A stone with a flash of blue
sections.body: Labradorite is a natural stone known for a blue iridescence that appears when light hits it at the right angle. Every piece is different. In an iwagumi-style scape it works as a statement stone, a single focal point against plain substrate and low plants.

Let the stone be the focus. Place it off centre, with the best face turned toward the viewing angle, and leave open space around it so the flash catches the light. Dim, warm light brings out the colour better than a very bright white bar. Choose a plain, dark substrate such as [aqua soil](/product/aqua-soil-planted-substrate) and a small number of fine-leaved plants.

Rinse the stone in clean water and scrub off dust with a soft brush. Do not use soap. Because it is a natural stone, test unfamiliar rock for hardness changes before using it in a soft-water or shrimp tank, by checking the water's pH and hardness after a few days.

faqs.q: Will it change my water hardness?
faqs.a: We have no test data for this stone, so test your own water after adding it. A soft-water shrimp tank is the place to be careful.

faqs.q: Will I get a piece like the photo?
faqs.a: Each piece is natural and different, so the shape and the blue flash will vary.

sections.h: A first food for tiny fry
sections.body: Brine shrimp eggs have a hard shell, and hatching them takes time and equipment. Decapsulation removes the shell, so tiny fry can eat the eggs directly from the tub with nothing to hatch. They suspend in the water column where fry hunt, and they are often the food that gets fussy fish eating again.

Feed a pinch at a time, once or twice a day, into a small tank or grow-out box such as an [acrylic breeder box](/product/acrylic-breeder-box-hang-on). Uneaten eggs are harmless but wasteful, and they can foul small volumes of water, so siphon leftovers. Mix a pinch in a little tank water first so that the eggs spread out rather than clump.

They suit the fry of egg layers and livebearers, shrimplets and small, fussy adults. As the fry grow, move on to crushed flake or micro pellets, so that they get a mixed diet. Keep the tub sealed and dry, since moisture ruins the eggs.

faqs.q: Do I need to hatch them?
faqs.a: No. Decapsulated eggs are fed straight from the tub, with no hatching.

faqs.q: How much should I feed?
faqs.a: A pinch per feeding. Fry have small stomachs, so feed small amounts often and clean up what is left.

sections.h: A grazing plate for the colony
sections.body: A spinach-and-mineral tablet that grows a fine biofilm after a day in the tank. That fuzz is what the colony actually grazes, adults and shrimplets alike. Drop a piece in and the shrimp gather on it for hours, which is also a good way to watch the colony and count berried females.

Break the tablet and use a piece, not the whole thing. Shrimp eat very little, so the rule is less than you think. Remove any piece that is still there after a day or two, since leftover food fouls the water. Feed one or two times a week alongside the biofilm that already grows in the tank, and skip a feed if the shrimp are not interested.

Shrimp moult to grow, and moulting depends on minerals in the food and the water. The tablet supports that, as does a stable supply of food in a mature tank with plants, [catappa leaves](/product/catappa-leaves-indian-almond) and moss. Colour-enhancing ingredients deepen reds in cherry shrimp over regular use.

faqs.q: Should I crush it or drop it in whole?
faqs.a: Break it into pieces. A small piece is easier to eat and easier to remove if it is not finished.

faqs.q: How often should I feed it?
faqs.a: Once or twice a week is plenty in a mature tank with biofilm and plants. Overfeeding is a common cause of poor water in shrimp tanks.

sections.body: Bettas are top dwellers and like to rest near the surface. A silk leaf on a suction mount gives them a place to lounge, sleep and patrol from. If your betta naps on the filter intake or lies on the substrate, this is a simple upgrade. Males also build bubble nests under and around the leaf.

Mount it close to the surface so the fish can lie on it with its head near the air. Keep it clear of the filter outflow, and away from any strong flow that would push it around. The silk is soft, with no sharp edges, so it is safe for veil tails and big fins. You can move it as the water level or the fish's preference changes.

A hammock works best with live plants, a lid so that the air above the surface stays warm, and gentle flow. A small [sponge filter](/product/bio-sponge-filter-4-pack) or a low-flow [USB filter](/product/nano-hang-on-filter-usb) keeps the water calm.

faqs.q: Will my betta use it?
faqs.a: Most do, though some take a few days. Place it near where the fish already rests.

faqs.q: Can other fish use it?
faqs.a: It is made for bettas, but other surface-loving fish may rest on it.

sections.body: The bundle packs together three things a new planted tank needs: the [Aurora 48 LED bar](/product/aurora-48-planted-tank-led) (48 cm), a five-piece stainless [scaping tool set](/product/aquascaping-tool-set-5-piece) and 8-in-1 [test strips](/product/test-strips-8-in-1-100-count). It suits a first planted tank that is 48 to 61 cm wide (measure the outside of the rim, as with the light on its own).

It does not include the tank, substrate, filter, heater, plants or CO2. Plan those separately. A common starting point is a rimless tank with [aqua soil](/product/aqua-soil-planted-substrate), low-light plants such as anubias and java fern, and a small filter. Use the [tank-size pages](/tanks) to work out heater wattage, flow and substrate for your tank.

Set the light timer to six hours at first and raise it slowly. Cycle the tank before you add fish and use the strips each week to track ammonia, nitrite and nitrate. The tools help you place and trim plants without disturbing the substrate.

faqs.q: Is the light the same as the Aurora 48 sold on its own?
faqs.a: Yes, the bundle includes the Aurora 48 LED bar, so the same fit range and features apply.

faqs.q: What else do I need for a first planted tank?
faqs.a: A tank, substrate, a filter, a heater for tropical fish, plants and a dechlorinator for tap water. The tank-size pages on this site list the heater and flow for common sizes.

sections.body: The set has straight tweezers, curved tweezers, straight scissors, curved scissors and a substrate spatula, all stainless steel. Tweezers place stems and moss precisely, scissors trim, and the spatula smooths substrate and pushes it into place. Together they cover the main jobs in a planted tank.

Use tweezers to grip stems low down, close to the base, and push them into the substrate at a slight angle. Curved scissors let you trim carpets flush and cut along the line of the substrate, and straight scissors suit stem tops and cutting at the back of the scape. Use the spatula to level soil after planting, rather than your fingers.

Rinse the tools in clean water and dry them after each use, and they will last for years. The set comes in a bag, with three packing options (colour box, drawstring pouch, canvas roll). For longer reach in a deep tank, add [long-reach tweezers](/product/long-reach-tweezers-30cm).

faqs.q: Will the tools rust?
faqs.a: They are stainless steel, which resists rust in fresh water. Rinse and dry them after use for the longest life.

faqs.q: Do I need long tweezers as well?
faqs.a: For a deep tank, yes. A longer tool keeps your hands out of the water.

sections.body: In a deep tank, short tweezers force your whole forearm into the water, which disturbs fish and clouds the substrate. These long stainless tweezers keep your hands dry and let you reach the back corner of the scape. The fine machined tips grip stems and moss without crushing.

Options are straight and curved. Straight tips are for general planting and precise placement. Curved tips are better for reaching around hardscape and planting at an angle. If you are unsure, start with straight. The length is listed per option, so check the one you select.

Grip the stem close to the base, and push it into the substrate at a slight angle. Release the tweezers as you pull them out, so that you do not take the plant with them. For moss, tie or glue it to rock or wood first. For trimming, add a pair of [curved spring scissors](/product/curved-spring-scissors).

faqs.q: Are they stainless?
faqs.a: Yes. They are stainless steel and suit regular use in fresh water.

sections.body: The curved blade sits parallel to the substrate when you hold the handle level, so carpet plants such as Monte Carlo, dwarf hairgrass and glosso come out flush, without divots. The spring return opens the blades between cuts, so a long trimming session is less tiring and you can work one-handed.
Options are 21 cm curved, 25 cm curved and 25 cm wave. The longer 25 cm length reaches further into a deeper tank. The blades are 4 mm thick 304 stainless.

Trimmed leaves float and spread, so collect them with a net after each trim, or you will see them settle on the carpet and rot. Do a water change after a big trim. Dry the scissors and wipe them with a clean cloth to keep the spring working, and add the matching [tweezers](/product/long-reach-tweezers-30cm) for replanting.

faqs.q: Which size should I choose?
faqs.a: The 21 cm pair suits shallow and nano tanks. The 25 cm pair reaches further into deeper tanks, so choose it if your hand would otherwise go well under the water.

faqs.q: Are they safe in a planted tank?
faqs.a: They are 304 stainless steel, which is suited to regular use in fresh water. Rinse and dry them after each session.

sections.h: Pick the size by glass thickness
sections.body: Magnetic cleaners only work when the magnet is strong enough to hold the two halves together through the glass. Choose by thickness and tank size: up to 4 mm for 20 to 35 cm tanks, up to 6 mm for 35 to 60 cm, up to 10 mm for 60 to 90 cm and up to 12 mm for tanks 100 cm and over. Measure the glass if you are not sure.

If the two halves separate, the inner half floats to the surface instead of sinking into the substrate, so it never gets buried or drags grit across the glass. A blade attachment deals with stubborn spot algae. Pass it slowly, with steady pressure, and stop if it catches on grit.

Clean weekly, before algae gets hard, and stay above the substrate line. If algae keeps returning in a few days, the cause is usually too many hours of light or surplus nutrients. A shorter photoperiod and a regular water change fix that faster than more scrubbing. For several cleaning heads on one handle, see the [5-in-1 cleaning set](/product/5-in-1-tank-cleaning-set).

faqs.q: Does it scratch glass?
faqs.a: Not if the pad is clean. Rinse it if it picks up grit and stay clear of the substrate.

faqs.q: What if I choose the wrong size?
faqs.a: A magnet that is too weak will not hold through the glass, and one that is too strong traps grit. Match the size to your glass thickness.
